newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's government wins praise for economy in polls.
newsitem.headline: Spain's government wins praise for economy in polls.

text.p: Nearly one year after taking power, Spain's Popular Party government won solid marks for its economic policies, but voters were less pleased on the political front, according to two polls published on Sunday.

"Those citizens that see a positive evolution in the economy are double those who perceive a worsening, and for the first time, a significant percentage of Spaniards (14 percent) said they had noticed improvement in their financial condition,"one of them, appearing in the newspaper El Pais, found.
The conservatives have presided over dramatic drops in inflation and interest rates since they formed a government on May 5, 1996, having put an end to 13 years of socialist rule.
In the poll, they earned the greatest praise for economic policies, and were regarded as conciliatory and responsible.
But their overall style was seen as weak and they were faulted for failing to inspire confidence, according to the representative survey conducted by Demoscopia.
"The assessment of economic policy does not result in improved ratings overall for the government which continues to earn just a passing grade," El Pais said.
According to the poll's voter intentions, the conservatives lost ground absolutely but they closed part of their gap to the leading opposition Socialists.

Twenty-one percent of the electorate would now vote for the conservatives, down from 22.1 in the January survey, the survey showed. The socialists lost yet more voters. Now 22.5 percent would opt for them compared with 25.3 percent in January.

In a separate representative poll in daily El Mundo, those surveyed also expressed satisfaction with the government's economic accomplishments, pointing specifically to the decline in interest rates and the reduction in public expenditure.

But they were less pleased with the government's new hard-line stance toward Cuba, or its decision last summer against opening secret files that could implicate the former government in the 1980s "dirty war" against Basque guerrillas.

In the Sigma Dos survey, 67.3 percent applauded the decline in rates and 65.2 percent the reduction in public expenditure. But a plurality of 39.5 percent was displeased by the PP's Cuba policy, and 48.7 percent by the failure to declassify the spy documents.
